title: perf: Cache `Version` hash value in dedicated slot
head: 1676a10cdad3f6183dc7f738d3a30950c67199a4

families.why: The new version adds a _hash_cache slot and caches the hash value on first __hash__ call. When the same Version objects are hashed repeatedly (e.g., used repeatedly as dict/set keys), the cached hash avoids recomputing the comparison key and its hash, giving a speedup.
families.size_meaning: Number of distinct version strings created; each will be hashed many times in the benchmark.

families.why: The change adds a cached ``_hash_cache`` attribute and makes ``__hash__`` return the cached value on subsequent calls. Workloads that create a modest number of ``Version`` objects and then hash them repeatedly (e.g. using versions as dictionary keys or set members) should see a speed‑up because the hash is computed only once per object.
families.size_meaning: Number of distinct version objects created; each will be hashed many times in the benchmark.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # Produce *n* distinct but simple version strings (fast‑path parser).
    # Each call to the constructor receives a single‑element list.
    base = "1.0."
    return [[base + str(i)] for i in range(1, n + 1)]

families.why: The change adds a cached ``_hash_cache`` on ``Version``.  Objects that are hashed repeatedly (e.g. used as dict keys or put into a set and looked‑up many times) now pay the hashing cost only once; subsequent ``__hash__`` calls return the cached integer.
families.size_meaning: n = number of distinct version strings inserted into a set/dict and then looked‑up n times each
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # generate n distinct, simple version strings (fast‑path)
    rng = random.Random(0xC0FFEE)
    versions = [f"{rng.randint(0,9)}.{rng.randint(0,9)}.{rng.randint(0,9)}" for _ in range(n)]
    # each version will be inserted into a set and then looked‑up n times
    # the benchmark will create Version objects from these strings
    return [[v] for v in versions]

families.why: The new version adds a _hash_cache attribute that is initialised to None in __init__, from_parts and __replace__. The cold‑sort benchmark creates many Version objects, clears _key_cache (and now also clears _hash_cache) before each sort, and then sorts them using only rich comparisons (__lt__). The extra attribute write on construction and the extra attribute clear in the benchmark add overhead while providing no benefit because __hash__ is never called during sorting.
families.size_meaning: Number of distinct version strings to parse and sort; larger n means more objects and a longer sort.

families.why: The new ``_hash_cache`` slot adds an extra attribute write in ``__init__`` (``self._hash_cache = None``) and in ``__new__`` paths (``from_parts``, ``__replace__``). When a program creates many short, pure‑numeric versions (the fast‑path parser that splits on ‘.’) but never hashes them, the extra attribute write and the larger ``__slots__`` layout add overhead to every construction.
families.size_meaning: Number of simple ``X.Y.Z`` version strings parsed via the fast‑path.

families.why: The fast‑path parser now has to initialise an extra ``_hash_cache`` slot (and set it to ``None``) on every ``Version`` constructed from a simple ``X.Y.Z`` string.  When many simple versions are created but never hashed, the extra attribute initialisation and the extra ``self._hash_cache = None`` store add overhead.
families.size_meaning: n = number of simple ``X.Y.Z`` version strings to construct
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    rng = random.Random(0xBEEF)
    # simple dot‑only versions hit the fast‑path parser
    return [[f"{rng.randint(0,9)}.{rng.randint(0,9)}.{rng.randint(0,9)}"] for _ in range(n)]

families.family: Invalid version strings that nevertheless contain indicator characters (e.g. a trailing dot followed by a letter). The fast‑path still does the full scan before the regex fails.
families.why: Even though the version is invalid, the extra disjoint check runs; the regex then fails. This is the single allowed invalid family.
families.size_meaning: Number of dotted segments before the malformed tail.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # "1." repeated n times then an alphabetic tail – not a valid PEP‑440 version
    version = "1." * n + "x"
    return [(version,)]

families.family: invalid strings that look simple (only digits and dots) but contain a non‑numeric segment, e.g. "1.2.x"
families.why: The indicator set is disjoint, so the fast path is entered. The code then executes `tuple(map(int, version.strip().split('.')))`, which raises `ValueError` on the bad segment; the exception is caught and re‑raised as `InvalidVersion`. Exception handling is considerably slower than the original regex‑only failure path.
families.size_meaning: n = number of leading numeric segments before the bad segment; larger n makes the split and the failed `int` conversion traverse more items before the exception.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # build "1.1.1....1.x" with n numeric parts then a non‑numeric "x"
    good = ".".join("1" for _ in range(n))
    version = f"{good}.x"
    return [[version]]

families.family: Each numeric chunk increases digit count linearly while keeping total chunks fixed
families.why: The fast‑path’s `isdisjoint` test iterates over every character. For a long dotted release the string length grows with n, so the extra scan adds linear overhead before the (already linear) regex match.
families.size_meaning: Number of dotted release segments (plus the trailing pre‑release).

families.why: The fast‑path’s `isdisjoint` test iterates over every character. For a long dotted release the string length grows with n, so the extra scan adds linear overhead before the (already linear) regex match.

def make(n):
    release = ".".join(["999"] * n)
    version = f"{release}c5"
    return [(version,)]
